why_interesting.text: The main job is an arrow the person follows, with GPS as a backup for the carer. On 23 March 2026 ONS Magazine described the same device and called the brothers product developers. The site is still taking reservations for delivery at the end of December 2026.

name: Ally Labs
summary: Listens in care-home bedrooms and alerts staff at night.

scene.job: It is a smart home.

deep_dive.product: A smart home.

title: Ally Labs
research_summary: a smart home.
job: Ally puts a Wi-Fi monitor in a care-home bedroom. It uses sound and motion to separate a resident's activity from ordinary background noise, then alerts staff in an app when someone calls for help, gets up, seems restless, or may be in discomfort. Teams use it at night so they can answer those alerts instead of walking in for routine checks. The Local Government Association says the sensor builds a behaviour profile over about two weeks, and homes are told to switch it off during the day.
who_pays: Care homes are the buyer. Ally does not publish a list price. It says homes typically see a 7x return, and the site has a calculator based on bed count and the night-check schedule. In Dorset, the Digitising Social Care programme funded the pilot. Ally's own account of that programme says each participating home received £10,000.

status.text: Companies House lists Ally Labs Limited as active, with accounts made up to 31 August 2025, at Naldretts Court, Wisborough Green. The product site was still selling the bedroom monitor. No news found in the last 12 months.

traction.text: On 3 February 2025 the Local Government Association wrote that six Dorset homes were due to receive 184 Ally sensors. Ally's site cites research claiming 63 percent fewer bedroom falls. Companies House incorporated Ally Labs Limited on 10 November 2015. No funding round was found.

who_pays.text: Care homes are the buyer. No public price. It is sold by direct sales, and the site has a calculator based on bed count and the night-check schedule. In Dorset, the Digitising Social Care programme funded a pilot of 184 sensors. No family reimbursement route was found.

what_it_does.text: Ally puts a Wi-Fi monitor in a care-home bedroom. Sound and motion trigger an app alert when a resident calls for help, gets up, or may be in discomfort, so night teams can skip routine checks. Homes are told to switch it off during the day.

why_interesting.text: Thomas Tredinnick co-founded Ally and is chief executive. A Care Management Show speaker note says he was formerly an aerospace engineer and founded Ally Cares to address staff challenges in UK homes. The product is aimed at the night round.

competitors.name: cogvis
competitors.difference: Unlike cogvis, which spots falls in care homes without camera pictures, Ally uses a bedroom monitor that listens and senses motion, and the Local Government Association says homes are told to switch it off during the day.

competitors.name: OSO-AI
competitors.difference: Compared with OSO-AI, which spots falls and distress in nursing homes so staff can respond, Ally is sold to UK care homes for the night round and says it files notes into the home's digital care record.

job: Merci Prosper arranges a partial sale for homeowners over 60. Its property company, Foncière Prosper, buys between 10% and 50% of the home in front of a notary. The owner keeps living there and receives the money as a lump sum or a monthly payment, while an occupation fee is paid as extra shares in the home. It is not a life annuity and not a loan.
who_pays: The homeowner sells a share to Foncière Prosper. There is no fixed public price: the cash depends on the value of the home and the share sold, between 10% and 50%. The owner can later buy that share back, sell the whole home, or pay an occupation fee for staying on.

who_pays.text: The homeowner sells a share to Foncière Prosper. There is no fixed public price: the cash depends on the value of the home and the share sold, between 10% and 50%. The owner can later buy that share back, sell the whole home, or pay an occupation fee for staying on.

traction.text: On 22 August 2026, M6's midday news followed customers Corinne and Charles-André, owners of their house for 28 years, who sold 30% to pay off a loan and help their daughter. Merci Prosper is registered in Paris as RCS 899 841 290, with activity from 18 May 2021, and says Foncière Prosper holds French ESUS social-utility approval. No count of signed contracts is published.

why_interesting.text: Many older owners have a valuable home and little spare cash, and a classic life annuity means giving up the whole house and the chance to leave it to children. Here the owner sells only a slice, stays, and can buy the slice back later. The company says the property fund's social purpose is checked each year under French ESUS rules.

what_it_does.text: CARU care is a home emergency alarm from CARU AG in Zurich. A person can call for help with a wrist or neck button, with a fall sensor in that button, or by saying help. The base unit can also remind someone to drink and to open a window when the air is stuffy. It connects over the mobile network or Wi-Fi to an alarm centre.

who_pays.text: Care organisations install it and connect it to their own alarm centre. CARU says people with a recognised care grade in Germany get the same care-fund subsidy as a standard home alarm, €27 including VAT. The device is listed in the German care-aid directory as number 52.40.01.1116.

traction.text: CARU names deployments with Volkssolidarität Chemnitz, the German Red Cross in Paderborn, and the Bavarian Red Cross in Erding and Würzburg. The company says 90% of users turn on fall detection and 80% use a health reminder. The Swiss register still shows the company at Weberstrasse 3 in Zurich, with a capital update on 9 December 2025.

why_interesting.text: A classic home alarm does nothing if the person cannot reach the button. CARU adds a fall sensor and a spoken call, and the German care-aid list accepted the device in July 2022 as a home alarm that works over a mobile SIM or a home router. It is a box in the house, not software for running a care home.

status.text: The product site is live, and the Swiss commercial register shows CARU AG still seated in Zurich, with a statute and capital filing on 9 December 2025.

job: Essence SmartCare sells MDsense, a wall-mounted radar that looks for a fall indoors and does not need the person to wear a pendant. The product page says it works in the dark, can be used near bathing areas, tells people from pets up to 30 kilograms, and covers a room of up to 4 by 4 metres. It is meant to connect to the company's Care@Home alarm service for homes and senior residences. A 2020 launch notice says the sensor has no video and no sound.
who_sells: Used by seniors at home and retirement facilities.
who_pays: The pages describe MDsense for independent living and for senior care facilities, sold with Care@Home to care providers. No public unit price was found.

what_it_does.text: Essence SmartCare sells MDsense, a wall-mounted radar that looks for a fall indoors and does not need the person to wear a pendant. The product page says it works in the dark, can be used near bathing areas, tells people from pets up to 30 kilograms, and covers a room of up to 4 by 4 metres. It is meant to connect to the company's Care@Home alarm service for homes and senior residences. A 2020 launch notice says the sensor has no video and no sound.

who_pays.text: The pages describe MDsense for independent living and for senior care facilities, sold with Care@Home to care providers. No public unit price was found.

traction.text: Essence SmartCare announced MDsense on 11 September 2020 and said its own research found that less than half of people in residential care wear a fall detector. In June 2021 the product won Connected World's IoT Innovations Award. A later product page says the fall model was trained on more than 20,000 body positions. The parent, Essence Group, said in 2020 that it had 50 million devices deployed. That is a group figure, not a count of MDsense units. The head office is in Herzliya, Israel, with offices in London, Hoboken, and Madrid.

why_interesting.text: A pendant only helps if the person is wearing it, and Essence says fewer than half of residential-care residents do. The radar watches the room instead, without a camera. The published coverage is only 4 by 4 metres, so each room that should be watched, including the bathroom, needs its own sensor.

status.text: The MDsense product page is still published, and the contact page lists a head office in Herzliya plus offices in the UK, the US, and Spain. Essence SmartCare is part of Essence Group.
